tip: ‘cafodd’ plus ‘ei’ plus a verb-noun is the past passive: ‘cafodd y bont ei difrodi’ means the bridge was damaged.
‘gan’ softens the word after it: ‘Llywodraeth’ becomes ‘gan Lywodraeth’.
Feminine ‘ei’ (her) adds h to a word starting with a vowel: ‘adeiladu’ becomes ‘ei hadeiladu’.
After masculine ‘ei’ (his), t softens to d: ‘traethawd’ becomes ‘ei draethawd’.
The thing a past-tense verb acts on takes soft mutation: ‘tractor’ becomes ‘dractor’ in ‘Prynodd Iolo dractor newydd’.
Number words like third match feminine nouns: ‘trydydd’ becomes ‘drydedd’ in ‘y drydedd ganrif’.
After ‘fy’ (my), g becomes ng: ‘goruchwyliwr’ becomes ‘fy ngoruchwyliwr’.
‘pe bai’ plus ‘wedi’ makes a past hypothetical: ‘pe bai'r polisi wedi'i weithredu’ means if the policy had been implemented.
A feminine singular noun soft-mutates a following adjective: after ‘gath’, ‘du’ becomes ‘ddu’.
Welsh builds the passive with ‘cael ei’ plus the verb-noun: ‘cael ei hadrodd’ means it is being told.
The word ‘ei’ meaning his soft-mutates what follows: after ‘ei’, ‘bai’ becomes ‘fai’.
The ‘-odd’ ending marks the past tense for he, she or it: ‘cyrhaeddodd’ means arrived.
Before an adjective the linking ‘yn’ soft-mutates it: ‘yn fyr’ comes from ‘byr’.
‘pe bawn i’ sets up an unreal, hypothetical if: ‘pe bawn i wedi gwybod’ means if I had known.
A feminine singular noun soft-mutates after ‘y’: ‘dinas’ becomes ‘y ddinas’.
‘am’ soft-mutates the word after it: ‘cerdd’ becomes ‘gerdd’ in ‘am gerdd’.
Welsh shows possession by placing nouns side by side: ‘dyfodol yr iaith’ means the language's future.
The ‘-wch’ ending gives a command to more than one person, or a polite one: ‘neidiwch’ means jump.
The ‘-wyd’ ending makes a past passive: ‘enillwyd’ means was won, and you can name the doer with ‘gan’, as in ‘gan fyfyriwr’ (by a student).
‘ar ôl’ plus a verb-noun means after doing something: ‘ar ôl cwblhau’ means after completing.
‘prif’ comes before its noun and soft-mutates it: ‘canfyddiadau’ becomes ‘prif ganfyddiadau’.
‘yn’ meaning in triggers nasal mutation and itself becomes ‘ym’: ‘pob’ turns into ‘ym mhob’.
The word ‘â’ (with) triggers aspirate mutation: ‘canfyddiadau’ becomes ‘â chanfyddiadau’.
The ending ‘-wraig’ marks a female doer: ‘sgriptiwraig’ means a woman scriptwriter.
‘o’ (of) soft-mutates the word after it: ‘tasgau’ becomes ‘o dasgau’.
Fronting the adjective, ‘hir yw’, adds emphasis, common in proverbs. Neutral order is ‘mae pob aros yn hir’, all waiting is long.
Add ‘-ach’ for the comparative: ‘iach’ means healthy, so ‘bwyta'n iachach’ means to eat healthier.
To bring is ‘dod â’, literally come with. Here ‘dod â diodydd’ means bring drinks.
Welsh has no verb to have: ‘mae beic coch gan Megan’ is literally a red bike is with Megan, meaning Megan has one.
After ‘mae gen i’, I have, the thing owned soft-mutates: ‘teulu’ becomes ‘deulu’ in ‘gen i deulu’.
